candidate.answerReason: A square is covered exactly when its farthest corner is within the disc. In each quadrant, the allowable positive integer corner coordinates give 3 + 3 + 2 + 0 = 8 squares, for 32 altogether.

methods.label: Count farthest corners in one quadrant
methods.explanation:
Use the side of one checkerboard square as the unit of length. The board then has side length \(8\), and the disc has radius \(4\). Because the board has eight rows and columns, its two central grid lines divide it into four congruent \(4\times4\) blocks. Symmetry lets us count one block and multiply by four.

Put the origin at the common center, with the coordinate axes along those central grid lines. In the first quadrant, label a square by its farthest corner \((i,j)\), where \(i,j\in\{1,2,3,4\}\). Every point \((u,v)\) of this square satisfies \(0\le u\le i\) and \(0\le v\le j\), so its squared distance from the center is at most \(i^2+j^2\). Thus the entire square is covered exactly when
\[
i^2+j^2\le 16.
\]
For \(i=1\), the possible values of \(j\) are \(1,2,3\). For \(i=2\), they are again \(1,2,3\). For \(i=3\), they are \(1,2\), and for \(i=4\), there are none. These lists include every square in the block exactly once.

There are therefore \(3+3+2=8\) covered squares per block. Each checkerboard square has its interior in exactly one of the four blocks, so the total is
\[
4\cdot8=\boxed{32},
\]
choice \(\text{E}\).
